title: Effect of thermal adaptation on seasonal outdoor thermal comfort
central_proposition: Thermal adaptation significantly influences seasonal outdoor thermal comfort in hot-humid regions, leading to seasonal shifts in neutral and preferred temperatures and divergent thermal preferences for identical thermal comfort index exposures.

concept_definitions.name: Thermal adaptation
concept_definitions.definition: Contextual factors including thermal experience, comfort expectations, perceived thermal control, culture and duration of exposure that affect thermal perceptions and preferences beyond the energy balance of the human body.

concept_definitions.name: Neutral temperature
concept_definitions.definition: The temperature coinciding with the central thermal sensation (TSV = 0) in the ASHRAE 7-point scale, at which people feel neither cool nor warm.

concept_definitions.name: Preferred temperature
concept_definitions.definition: The thermal environmental condition under which individuals prefer neither warmer nor cooler temperatures.

concept_definitions.name: Standard Effective Temperature (SET*)
concept_definitions.definition: A physiologically relevant index integrating air temperature (Ta), vapour pressure (VP) or relative humidity (RH), mean radiant temperature (Tmrt) and air speed (v).

argument_structure: The study empirically investigates the effect of thermal adaptation on seasonal outdoor thermal comfort in central Taiwan through field surveys and concurrent microclimatic measurements. It analyzes seasonal variations in clothing, neutral and preferred temperatures, and preferences for humidity, sunshine, and wind. Finally, it quantifies the relative contributions of microclimatic parameters to thermal perception to demonstrate the influence of adaptation.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Thermal adaptation operates through behavioral adjustments (e.g., clothing) and psychological shifts (e.g., altered comfort expectations based on seasonal experience). These adaptive processes lead to different thermal comfort requirements and preferences across seasons, even when objective thermal comfort indices (like SET*) are identical, indicating that subjective comfort is not solely determined by the body's energy balance.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Basic thermal comfort requirements (neutral and preferred temperatures) will vary significantly between hot and cool seasons in hot-humid regions.

Subjects' thermal preferences for temperature, humidity, sunshine, and wind will diverge between seasons even under identical thermal comfort index (SET*) exposures, indicating the influence of thermal adaptation.

Operative temperature (To) will be the dominant microclimatic parameter influencing thermal perception (TSV), while air speed and humidity will have lesser contributions, particularly in hot-humid climates.
bridge_warrants: The study connects thermal adaptation to psychological and behavioral factors, extending the understanding of thermal comfort beyond purely physiological energy balance models.

It compares findings from a hot-humid climate (Taiwan) with those from temperate (UK) and subtropical (Australia) climates, highlighting how annual temperature variation influences the magnitude of thermal adaptation effects.
It differentiates between 'neutral' and 'preferred' temperatures, suggesting a semantic artifact that influences subjective comfort assessments, linking to dual-process evaluation.
methodological_critiques: The paper notes that the choice of group division for ANOVA (too many or too few groups) can impact the representativeness of thermal sensations or the detectability of significant differences among groups.
limitations: The annual variation of air temperature in Taiwan (approx. 15°C) is smaller than in UK (28°C) and Australia (31°C), which may explain the smaller observed shifts in neutral temperature compared to those regions.
Wind speed (0.8-1.2 m/s) and relative humidity (70-80%) are relatively stable throughout the year in central Taiwan, which may limit their relative contribution to thermal sensation variance.
Social norms may limit further clothing removal even when air temperatures exceed 28°C, potentially affecting the full range of behavioral adaptation observed.

paper_metadata.title: Expert and exceptional performance: evidence of maximal adaptation to task constraints.
paper_metadata.crossref_title: EXPERT AND EXCEPTIONAL PERFORMANCE: Evidence of Maximal Adaptation to Task Constraints
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: ▪ Abstract  Expert and exceptional performance are shown to be mediated by cognitive and perceptual-motor skills and by domain-specific physiological and anatomical adaptations. The highest levels of human performance in different domains can only be attained after around ten years of extended, daily amounts of deliberate practice activities. Laboratory analyses of expert performance in many domains such as chess, medicine, auditing, computer programming, bridge, physics, sports, typing, juggling, dance, and music reveal maximal adaptations of experts to domain-specific constraints. For example, acquired anticipatory skills circumvent general limits on reaction time, and distinctive memory skills allow a domain-specific expansion of working memory capacity to support planning, reasoning, and evaluation. Many of the mechanisms of superior expert performance serve the dual purpose of mediating experts' current performance and of allowing continued improvement of this performance in response to informative feedback during practice activities.
